name: IPL hair removal device

lead: An IPL hair removal device is a home flash lamp that emits broad-spectrum pulsed light to reduce unwanted body and facial hair over a series of sessions. It is a consumer version of systems used in clinics, aimed at smoother skin with less regrowth.

Melanin in the hair absorbs the light and turns it into heat, which damages the follicle and pushes it into a resting phase. Reviews describe light-based hair reduction as effective in clinical settings, with the best results for dark hair on light skin. Evidence for home devices is smaller and shows more modest reductions than professional systems. The FDA definition of permanent reduction is a long-term, stable reduction in regrowth, not complete removal.

paras: People shave the area, then flash the device across it in a repeating schedule, with sessions spaced weeks apart and used for months. It suits dark hair on lighter skin best and is less effective on light hair. Many use it as a cheaper alternative to clinic treatments.

Side effects include redness, burns and pigment changes, especially on darker skin because skin melanin also absorbs light. Eye protection is advised. A Cochrane review of lasers and photoepilation found evidence mainly for short-term hair reduction, and permanence has not been established for home devices.

angle.text: Home IPL devices thin and remove body and facial hair over repeated sessions as a cheaper alternative to clinic treatments. Light absorbed by hair pigment heats the follicle and slows regrowth. Trials have measured hair-count reductions, with results varying by skin and hair color.

lead: An IPL hair removal device is a consumer flashlamp that emits broad-spectrum pulsed light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, to reduce unwanted body and facial hair over a series of sessions. It is a home-use version of intense pulsed light systems used in clinics. Melanin in the hair absorbs the light and converts it to heat, which damages the follicle. [1][2]

Reviews describe light-based hair reduction as effective in clinical settings, with the best results for dark hair on light skin, and note that most studies examine darker hair and fairer skin. The evidence for home devices is smaller and shows more modest reductions than professional systems. The U.S. FDA definition of permanent reduction is a long-term, stable reduction in hair regrowth, not complete removal. [1][3][4][5]
infobox: Dark hair, light to medium skin
Repeat sessions over months; occasional top-ups

paras: Intense pulsed light uses a linear xenon flashlamp, with filters that cut off shorter and longer wavelengths, and a cooled light guide that contacts the skin. Home devices apply smaller, lower-energy pulses and often include a skin-tone sensor. [1] IPL differs from laser hair removal, which uses coherent light of one wavelength. [1]

Wikipedia credits Shimon Eckhouse with inventing IPL in 1992 and founding ESC Medical to commercialize it, first for vascular lesions. FDA clearances followed in 1995 for vascular lesions, then for pigmented lesions and hair removal in 1996 and 1997. [1] Grokipedia also names dermatologists Mitchel Goldman and Richard Fitzpatrick as collaborators. [2] Home IPL devices were developed later, and their efficacy has been the subject of reviews. [1][3][4]

Light absorbed by melanin in the hair shaft and follicle heats it, an approach called selective photothermolysis. Only follicles in the growth phase are susceptible, so multiple sessions spaced weeks apart are used, with Wikipedia citing 8 to 10 treatments at 4 to 6 week intervals for clinic devices. Because skin melanin also absorbs light, treatment is more reliable on light skin and dark hair and less effective on light, red, grey or white hair. [1][2]

A 2013 review in Dermatologic Surgery concluded that alexandrite, diode, Nd:YAG and IPL devices support long-term hair reduction in clinic settings and that more research is needed on safety and efficacy of home devices. [5] A 2021 review states that all hair-removal methods except electrolysis are temporary and that most studies involve dark hair and fair skin. [4]

Wikipedia summarizes a 2006 comparison reporting about 67% hair reduction at six months for IPL, versus about 69% for alexandrite and 72% for diode lasers. A Cochrane review of laser and photoepilation reported short-term reductions with generally low-quality trials. [1][6]

For home devices, a 2019 review in Lasers in Surgery and Medicine examined why they work and how effective they are. [7] In a randomized comparison of a professional diode laser and a home IPL device on the underarm, in 15 women who completed six treatments, the laser achieved about 85 to 88% hair reduction and the home device about 46 to 52%, with mild pain and redness. [8] A 2025 split-body study of 84 participants compared a home IPL with a clinic broadband-light system. [3]

Side effects reported in IPL literature include redness, pain, swelling, burns and pigment changes, with higher risk of pigmentary complications on darker skin. [1][5] Manufacturers advise using IPL and laser devices on light to medium skin tones and avoiding photosensitizing medications and damaged skin. [1] Eye protection is advised for light devices.

The site rates home IPL as having strong, durable evidence for hair reduction. In appearance communities it is discussed for facial and body hair reduction, and device cost is high relative to other grooming gear.

Commonly discussed features include flash count, skin-tone sensors, cooling and suitability for particular skin tones and body areas. Product labels specify the skin-tone range and hair colours for which devices are intended.

Human studies of hair reduction include a Cochrane review of laser and photoepilation, systematic and narrative reviews of light-based devices, and comparisons of home IPL with professional systems. Home-device trials are small, and a randomized underarm comparison found lower reduction with the home IPL than with a clinic diode laser. [4][5][6][7][8][3] Separately, IPL has been tested in randomized trials for dry eye due to meibomian gland dysfunction and for acne, which are different uses. [9]
